title: Chapter 81: Children
html:
The mission description was written in the first person. Its narrator had hidden in the fifth cubicle to capture the red shadow that appeared at midnight, but what followed was left unsaid, giving Chen Ge ample room to imagine the worst.

He switched off his flashlight. The mission says a red shadow appears in the toilet at midnight, but those footsteps belong to two people walking side by side. Did the red shadow find a friend during its years trapped in this abandoned school?

The footsteps drew steadily closer to the second-floor toilet. According to the mission, Chen Ge should hide in the fifth cubicle, but that seemed far too dangerous. He would be trapping himself.

Maybe I should take the initiative.Chen Ge hid behind the toilet door. Whoever entered would receive a mallet to the head before anything else. He drew a deep breath, held it, and raised the weapon.

The footsteps grew clearer—two people running side by side, dangerously close to the second-floor toilet. The wait was torture. Chen Ge did not know what was outside, much less what it intended to do. He could only keep perfectly silent.

Several seconds later, the footsteps finally stopped before the toilet entrance.

Here they come!

Sweat slicked the hand gripping the mallet, and his heart raced impossibly fast. Outside, the storm raged on, rain seeping into the room and spreading across the floor.

Where are they?Chen Ge glanced over his shoulder, but no faces peered down at him as he had feared. His patience frayed. One hand on the doorknob, he prepared to look outside—then lightning tore across the sky, and in its brief glare he saw two shadows cast across the toilet floor.

They’re standing at the entrance!

His body locked in place. With his flashlight off, the toilet around him was utterly black.

The shadows were short, like two children.

He kept his guard up. After several seconds, the footsteps resumed. Instead of entering, however, their owners took the staircase beside the toilet down to the first floor.

They’re just leaving?Chen Ge slowly emerged from behind the door. The entrance stood empty.

The thing that stood at the door earlier felt like two children. This is different from the red shadow described by the black phone. Is this because too much time has passed since then, or did my early arrival at the school mess up the schedule?

Unable to find an answer, Chen Ge switched his flashlight back on and approached the fifth cubicle. Whatever else happened, he had to determine whether this was the mission site. The door opened on an old but otherwise ordinary stall.

Then the mission site must be in the third-floor toilet. Those two children went down to the first floor, so this is my chance.Chen Ge headed for the exit, but before he reached it, his phone rang. The number was unfamiliar.

Who could this be?Chen Ge had few friends, and those he had rarely called. After a moment’s hesitation, he retreated to a corner, closed the livestream, and answered. “Hello?”

“Are you Ru Xue’s classmate? I heard you met a strange boy whom you suspect may have a psychological disorder?” The voice on the other end was grave and assured.

“I did, and you are?”

“I’m Ru Xue’s father.” He San had mentioned passing Chen Ge’s number to Gao Ru Xue. Apparently, his senior worked fast.

“Could you describe the boy in more detail? Psychological illness can act like poison in the body. If left untreated, it may ruin his future.” Gao Ru Xue’s father understood the danger of psychological disorders. In his view, they could be more harmful than many physical diseases.

“There is this boy about seven or eight. He’s physically fine, but he appears to have withdrawn from the world; he refuses to interact with others and is afraid of sunlight.”

“Any other symptoms? Please be as specific as you can.”

“I met him outside a Haunted House attraction. His aunt said he likes spending time in Haunted Houses. He showed none of the fear or anxiety most people would feel—in fact, he seemed more comfortable in the dark than in sunlight. I got the impression that dark corners make him feel safe.” Chen Ge shared his suspicions. Had he not met the child himself, he would never have believed such a peculiar boy existed.

“A boy of seven or eight who likes to visit Haunted Houses? And doesn’t feel afraid?”

“Yes. He was even interested in an actor wearing corpse makeup.”

The line went silent for several seconds. “If the issue is simply a lack of fear, it could be related to autism or abnormal function of the amygdala.”

“I’m sorry, but I don’t think I understand.”

“Put simply, the amygdala helps process memory and emotional responses such as anger and fear. If it is damaged, a person might feel no fear even when facing a lion or a viper, let alone inside a Haunted House.”

Doctor Gao had a point, but the description did not quite fit Fan Yu. “It’s not that he isn’t afraid of anything. He fears sunlight and hates walking in it. And he wasn’t merely unafraid of the Haunted House—he liked being there. Inside and outside, he seemed like two different children.”

After a moment, Chen Ge added, “Outside, he was completely silent and refused to interact with anyone. Inside, he came alive. When it was time to go, he fought so hard to stay that I saw him injure his aunt.”

“Your description might also suggest bipolar disorder—destructive and irrational during manic episodes, withdrawn into his own world during depressive ones,” Doctor Gao said. “But one detail troubles me. Bipolar episodes can be triggered at any time; there should not be so clear a boundary between being inside and outside a Haunted House. Since that environment changes his behavior, the source of his problem may also be connected to one. Did he suffer trauma in a Haunted House when he was younger? Or did his parents work at one?”

Doctor Gao’s analysis sparked a new suspicion in Chen Ge’s mind.

The boy’s personality had changed inside Chen Ge’s Haunted House, and one thing set it apart from every other attraction: it was genuinely haunted.
